title: Four Ways Students Forget Things
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Drawing on Dan Willingham's model of the human learning system, Stuart walks through four distinct points at which forgetting can occur in a classroom: failure to attend to material in the first place, failure to retrieve information already in long-term memory, actual loss of information from long-term memory over time, a defragging process especially active during sleep, and failure to hold information in working memory long enough to process it into long-term storage. For each, he offers a practical response: reducing environmental and attentional competition, building in frequent retrieval practice, designing repeated exposure to material across a course, and being mindful that we remember what we think about, meaning working memory, not just attention, is the real gatekeeper to long-term retention. He illustrates the working-memory point with a hypothetical about trying to write an article during a staff meeting: even with some attention on the speaker, working memory consumed by another task would mean almost nothing from the meeting sticks.
points: Four distinct forgetting mechanisms, per Willingham: failure to attend, failure to retrieve from long-term memory, actual decay or removal from long-term memory, likened to computer defragging, especially during sleep, and failure to hold material in working memory long enough to encode it.
Practical fix for retrieval failure: frequent retrieval practice, giving students regular opportunities to pull previously learned material from long-term memory rather than re-reading it.

The working-memory point is the article's sharpest claim: attention alone doesn't guarantee learning; we remember what we think about, meaning what occupies working memory determines what gets encoded, not merely what a student is nominally paying attention to.

The staff-meeting thought experiment, attending to a speaker while mentally drafting an article, is used to show that partial attention plus working-memory hijacking produces near-total forgetting of the actual content, a dynamic directly relevant to distracted students in class.
quotes: First, students can forget things we do in class because they weren't attending to them. It's pretty straightforward — you can't remember what you don't pay attention to.

If a student's attention is preoccupied with thoughts of a crush or a hidden cell phone or a frustrating experience in first hour, that student is likely to struggle to remember what we do in class today because what we do has less of a chance to get through the attentional filter.

Second, students can forget things that are in long-term memory due to a failure to retrieve the information. The best way to remedy this is by giving them lots of opportunities to practice retrieving previously learned material.
The solution to this forgetting is making sure students are using and encountering information again and again in class.

Even though I tried paying attention to the PD, my working memory was mostly consumed with the article I was writing. What I had in mind during the meeting — what I was thinking about, what I was processing — wasn't the content of the PD, it was the task of writing the article.
Working memory is a key filter — they can't just pay attention, they also have to think.
